Title: Inside Falcon AI Gateway: One Control Point for AI Traffic
Context: Falcon AI Gateway, now generally available and included with CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian™, extends AI visibility and enforcement beyond the CrowdStrike Falcon® sensor
Full Text:
As AI agents move from answering questions to executing actions, seeing AI activity isn't enough. Security teams need to control it.

AI requests now come from employee assistants, coding agents, SaaS copilots, and custom applications and cloud workloads that call models directly through SDKs. Each of these requesters connects to model providers on its own, with its own credentials, models, and settings.

Falcon AI Gateway, now generally available and included with CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian™, extends AI visibility and enforcement beyond the CrowdStrike Falcon® sensor. It routes AI traffic through a centralized gateway to inspect prompts and responses, monitor usage, and enforce policy across managed and unmanaged devices.

One Control Point for Model Access, Usage, and Security

Discovery shows where unsanctioned AI is in use. Falcon AI Gateway adds a complementary approach: Make the approved path the only path.

Falcon AI Gateway authenticates each request, routes it to the right provider and model, applies usage limits, and applies Falcon Guardian policy both before the request reaches the provider and again when the response comes back.

Teams block direct connections to model providers using the network controls they already run, and route approved applications and workloads through Falcon AI Gateway. As a result, the AI traffic reaching providers from those workloads has passed through Falcon Guardian policy on the way. This doesn't discover or redirect AI traffic automatically; it gives teams a deliberate control point for the workloads they choose to route through it.

This allows teams to:

See: Traffic, models, tokens, and estimated spend in one place, with dashboards, request logs, and event data.

Adapt: Applications send requests to one gateway endpoint with one gateway key, using the API formats they already speak. Provider credentials stay in the gateway, and administrators can switch between connected model providers, such as Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, and Google Vertex AI, without reconfiguring every workload.

Control: Rate limits and budgets on requests, tokens, or estimated spend, scoped by application, user, team, model, or provider. Application keys suit services and shared workloads; personal keys attribute usage to an individual.

Secure: Falcon Guardian policy inspects prompts and responses routed through the gateway for risks such as prompt injection and sensitive data leakage.

Falcon AI Gateway and the Falcon sensor share one Falcon Guardian policy model, and each enforces where the policy sits. The sensor acts on the endpoint, including the local processes, files, and commands an agent runs. Falcon AI Gateway acts on traffic routed through it and can't stop local processes.

Because traffic flows through one point, AI Kill Switch in Falcon Guardian can cut off agents’ access to the model via the traffic routed through Falcon AI Gateway.

Falcon Guardian customers can find Falcon AI Gateway in the Falcon console under Falcon Experiences > AI Gateway. Developers connect an existing SDK or coding tool by changing the base URL to point at the gateway and using a gateway key.

Title: ThreatsDay: 59 Linux Kernel Bugs, Falcon Spyware, GSocket Backdoors + 17 More Stories
Context: The attackers have been found to gain access through compromised contractor accounts and leverage AI-generated PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands during later stages...
Full Text:
A search result isn't always safe. An access request isn't always harmless. And a familiar account doesn't always mean a familiar person is using it. Simple things to remember. Yet a surprising amount of this week's trouble starts right there.

Attackers are using fake websites, stolen access, and trusted tools to get into places they shouldn't be. AI is helping them build attacks faster, while also giving them new systems to target. Some intruders are staying hidden even after security holes are fixed. Others are moving stolen money through a maze of transactions. And researchers keep finding small coding mistakes that can cause much bigger problems. Different stories, but much of the trouble comes down to making something dangerous look normal.

There is some good news, too. Criminal servers have been seized, and a few defenses are getting stronger. Still, plenty of things are going wrong in ways that shouldn't be this easy. Here's what turned up this week.

The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out.

North Korea's crypto laundering network

How North Korea Is Laundering $.64B Stolen from Binance

The North Korean threat actors linked to the record-breaking theft of $6.43 billion from Binance are using a highly complex and clearly automated method to launder the illicit proceeds. "Since the theft it has used more than 20,000 wallets on 16 blockchains, at least 36 services and at least 65,000 transactions," Dr. Tom Robinson, Elliptic's founder and chief scientist, said. "Around $3.0 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly as ETH and BTC. A negligible amount has likely been cashed out." The attackers have also been observed creating six meme coins on the NEAR blockchain network (FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI, and SINU) to launder a slice of the ill-gotten funds, passing through about $430,000 of the stolen cryptocurrency. The goal is to disguise the path of money and make it harder to trace where the assets eventually end up. Other tactics used to make funds tracing more difficult include moving between blockchains through bridges and cross-chain swap services, swapping between assets on DEXs, hopping through lending vaults and liquid-staking services, and mixing bitcoin through coinjoins, and ETH and SOL through the Privacy Cash privacy pool. The Binance breach is by no means the first to affect a major cryptocurrency exchange, but it is the biggest ever by magnitude. North Korean spokesperson Kim Yo Jong denied the country's role in the attack, calling it an "absurd" effort to "damage the international image of the DPRK."

GSocket detections surge 356%

Attacks Leveraging GSocket Spike in 2026

Microsoft said it has observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open-source remote access tool, on internet-facing Linux servers to maintain access after the original vulnerabilities were addressed, turning a single web application compromise into persistent access. "Because GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block," Microsoft said. "Defenders should look for GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections on affected hosts, not treat application patching alone as complete remediation." According to telemetry data, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2% from March through August 2026, with most of them associated with PHP web applications, cPanel hosts, and Apache. The majority of targets of GSocket activity are in the education and research sector, followed by technology and communications, manufacturing, and government entities.

235 servers seized in Europol takedown

Europol Operation Dismantles GootLoader, CastleRAT, and StealC Infrastructure

Europol, along with global partners, has disrupted the criminal infrastructure behind GootLoader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware, seizing 235 servers and 257 domains. "The operation targeted 'cybercrime-as-a-service' models, where these tools enabled further crimes like ransomware attacks and data theft," Europol said. As part of the operation, authorities have identified over 6 million victim credentials. "The suspects were using these credentials, stolen from the victims after they infected them, to sell them and later be used for other cyber-attacks such as ransomware," Europol added.

Browser-based espionage targets governments

Hackers Deploy Falcon Browser Spyware to Monitor Government Emails and Steal Passwords

A command and control (C2) framework called Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē) has been found compromising victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. Falcon shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with PeckBirdy, another JavaScript C2 framework that came to light early this year. It's assessed that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework. "An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information: passwords, emails, session cookies, [and] communications." Falcon has also been used to deliver an implant dubbed Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel. The activity has targeted government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. "The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives," Unit 42 said.

59 Linux kernel bugs uncovered

Microsoft Flags 59 Linux Kernel Bugs

Microsoft said its scan of a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026 unearthed 26,502 raw findings using MDASH, which subsequently formed the basis for 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs. This includes working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, such as CVE-2026-64563. "CVE-2026-64563 is a one-line state-reset bug in rhashtable, the Linux kernel's shared resizable hash table," Microsoft said. "Because callers trust the object pointers returned by a table walk, this small library flaw enabled a stable local privilege escalation on Linux -- and affected Android with SELinux enforcing -- without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces."

AI-assisted espionage in Central Asia

Silent Lynx Hackers Use AI Agent to Steal 2,000+ Tajik Government Documents

An exposed Silent Lynx server has uncovered cyber espionage operations targeting Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure from April to October 2026. "The directory held the group's tooling alongside data from active intrusions into government and critical infrastructure organisations across the region, and the AI agent the operator relied on to run them," CloudSEK said. "We assess with medium confidence that the operator has a Kazakhstan nexus: the operation runs in Russian, and the operator's own test traffic came from a residential Kazakh connection, which supports existing vendor assessments. The collection priorities, spanning transport, defence correspondence and resource ministries in neighbouring states, point to regional intelligence gathering rather than financial motive."

Contractor access fuels ransomware attacks

Citrus Ransomware Hackers Abuse Contractor Access, VLESS Tunnels, and AI-Generated Scripts

A new Russian-speaking ransomware group called Citrus is targeting Windows systems in corporate environments. The attackers have been found to gain access through compromised contractor accounts and leverage AI-generated PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands during later stages of the intrusion. In an attempt to reduce visibility, the threat actor removes tools and output files after execution, clears command history, and deletes event logs. The group also disguises tools and related artifacts with benign-looking names to make them appear legitimate by using a trusted brand name. The ransomware is a Sn00py-family ransomware variant written in Go. On Windows systems, the malware encrypts user files and appends the .citrus extension, while taking steps to hinder recovery and incident response. Kaspersky said the activity shares several similarities with Toy Ghouls. "Citrus stands out for the way AI-generated content appears to support hands-on intrusion activity on compromised systems," said Stanislav Larinsky, Kaspersky Security Services expert. "In the cases we investigated, the attackers combined third-party account access, privilege-escalation attempts and domain-wide deployment techniques. These incidents show how limited contractor access can become a path to broader compromise if it is not tightly controlled and continuously monitored."

Malicious AI agents exploit OAuth consent

New BluePhishing Attack Tricks Microsoft Entra Users Into Granting AI Agents Cloud Access

Proofpoint has disclosed details of a new technique called BluePhishing that's described as the "next evolution of OAuth consent abuse," enabling bad actors to leverage agent identities like Microsoft Entra Agent ID for initial access. BluePhishing "socially engineer[s] victims into granting consent to a malicious agent blueprint for initial access," it said. "Analogous to app consent phishing where attackers use client credentials to gain initial access to a tenant, BluePhishing extends this technique to the agent ecosystem. By exploiting gaps in visibility and governance around emerging AI agent adoption, attackers can abuse one-time consent links to create agent identities in target tenants, obtain access tokens, and operate with the privileges assigned to those agents."

AI age checks expand worldwide

Meta Expands Teen Account Protections Globally

Meta has announced that it's expanding its AI age-estimation technology globally to automatically place millions of teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. "We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections," Meta said. "As a result, millions more teens across the world who use Instagram will receive these built-in protections, even if they've misrepresented their age." In Australia, Meta has opted to use Apple's age-range signal as another method to help understand age.

OAuth support for Exchange migrations

Microsoft Supports OAuth Authentication for On-Premises Exchange Mailbox Migrations

Microsoft 365 Mailbox Replication Service (MRS) has added support for OAuth as an authentication method when migrating mailboxes between Microsoft 365 and an on-premises Exchange environment. "Once OAuth for MRS is configured, tenant administrators can create an OAuth migration endpoint and use it in migration batches or in onboarding and offboarding move jobs," Microsoft said. "You can use this method in both hybrid and non-hybrid organizations."

NTLM signing hardened against relay attacks

Microsoft Enables NTLM Signing by Default in Windows to Reduce Relay Attacks

In more Microsoft-related news, the tech giant has incorporated additional protections into Windows starting November 10, 2026, that address CVE-2026-118737 (CVSS score: 8.1), a critical remote code execution flaw in Remote Procedure Call Runtime that could allow an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. "These updates represent the first phase of improvements to NTLM message signing," Microsoft said. "These changes help ensure that authenticated NTLM sessions always establish a cryptographic session key and negotiate real message signing, reducing exposure to relay attacks." To that end, Windows servers will begin requiring NTLM signing by default starting May 2027.

Exposed cloud credentials lingered 18 months

Entra ID Issue Impacting Planning Inspectorate Disclosed

Details have emerged about a now-patched security flaw affecting the Planning Inspectorate, an executive agency of the United Kingdom's Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG). The issue involved a complete Microsoft Entra ID application credential that was committed in plaintext to a GitHub repository. "Although removed from the branch, the commit was orphaned via a force push and remained retrievable via GitHub's raw object CDN for 18 months," ControlPlane said. The client secret was deleted about 20 minutes after responsible disclosure on August 26, 2026.

Fake software sites spread infostealer

SEO Poisoning Campaign Delivers Armorsteal

An SEO poisoning campaign is using fake websites impersonating the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool to distribute a Python-based malware called Armorsteal. "The installer deployed a Python 3.11 runtime environment and three main components providing remote access, surveillance, and information stealing capabilities, with the Python code protected by Pyarmor," Zscaler said. "The remote access component communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server, downloads additional modules, and executes remote tasks. The surveillance component logs keystrokes, monitors the clipboard, captures screenshots, and displays fake cryptocurrency wallet notifications. The information stealing component targets browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, saved passwords, SSH keys, and Steam data."

Localized phishing delivers banking trojan

Grandoreiro Campaign Targets LATAM

A new Grandoreiro banking malware campaign is targeting users across Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and Peru through country-specific phishing lures that are tailored to each region. "The campaign uses localized phishing lures, primarily in Spanish, with some observed using Portuguese even when targeting Spanish-speaking countries," Arctic Wolf said. "The phishing chain relies on recently registered domains and layered redirection to hinder detection. The final payload is retrieved through a Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) seeded with the current date. The downloaded ZIP archive uses a deeply nested folder structure populated with two legitimate PE files and two benign PDF documents. A VBScript file located in the archive's root directory acts as the primary payload, employing junk code and multiple layers of obfuscation before reconstructing and launching a Delphi-based loader." The loader masquerades as a PDF reader and is used to fetch and run the banking trojan.

AI search results targeted by scam sites

Indirect Prompt Injection Campaign for Investment Scam Sites

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said it detected an indirect prompt injection (IDPI) campaign across 26 domains. "These are attempting black-hat Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to game AI-powered search results," Unit 42 said. "Almost all of the 26 pages have very similar content, presenting as AI-powered digital asset trading platforms. These sites appear to be scam sites designed to collect user information. The injected prompt is set to be hidden from a regular web user but likely visible to an AI agent. These attacks intend to poison SEO and manipulate AI agents to eventually get users to visit these sites."

PyPI adds release verification signals

PyPI Announces Redesigned Project Pages with New Security Tab

The Python Package Index (PyPI) has added a security tab to its project pages, giving developers easy access to security signals. "The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from," PyPI said. "PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation."

100+ domains spread credential stealer

REVSTEALER's Growing Distribution Ecosystem

The information stealer known as RevStealer is being propagated as part of an "industrial-scale, financially motivated campaign" that uses game cheats and AI tools as lures. The payload is distributed through more than 100 interconnected domains, trojanized Electron applications masquerading as Anthropic's Claude Opus 5, and hijacked YouTube distribution channels, per Akatsuki Legion. "Once executed, the malware performs a ten-point weighted sandbox-evasion scoring routine, decrypts an AES-256-CBC in-memory payload, and leverages fourteen indirect syscall wrappers and FNV-1a API hashing to bypass user-mode hooks before systematically harvesting credentials from browsers, password managers, cryptocurrency wallets, Steam, Roblox, Battle.net, EA Desktop, and Minecraft; then exfiltrating the loot as streamed, encrypted typed records over HTTPS, with a resilient Polygon blockchain dead-drop resolver standing by as a fallback command-and-control channel," the independent adversary research group said.

AI infrastructure becomes an attack target

Threat Actors Target AI Infrastructure

Threat actors have increasingly targeted AI orchestration platforms over the past few months, according to Sekoia. This is because "they concentrate API keys, enterprise data, and access to external tools," it added. This includes Flowise, which has been affected by multiple security flaws like CVE-2025-59528 and CVE-2026-41264. In one exploitation attempt recorded in August 2026, a suspected Chinese-speaking actor abused legitimate Flowise functionality to conduct automated reconnaissance and attempted to hijack the LLM agent to serve as an offensive analysis vector against external targets. "The attacker attempted to turn the AI agent into an interactive offensive assistant, submitting real-world reconnaissance data (Nightingale/Redis infrastructure) to generate custom exploitation playbooks and target analysis," Sekoia said.

AI-built phishing kits multiply

Vibe-Coded Phishing Kits Emerge

LevelBlue has disclosed details of a family of phishing kits named BlackApex, DarkApex, SPY, XXX101-TOKEN, OGPARKER1, W1-TOKEN, and ALIBOBO-TOKEN that are used to facilitate device code phishing attacks using shared document lures. The findings once again demonstrate how AI can speed up the development of a convincing multi-brand phishing kit. "Across all of its lures, the source shows traits we associate with AI-generated code, whether from direct prompts to a language model or from a person working alongside an AI coding assistant," LevelBlue said. "The code, endpoints, and interface are the same across all of them. We cannot say whether these names reflect separate operators, resellers or customers of a single kit, but the pattern is consistent with a shared product being rebranded and redeployed."

AI verifies Signal security properties

DeepMind's AlphaProof Code Proves the Signal Protocol Is Secure

Google's DeepMind has introduced AlphaProof Code, which brings together human experts and AI agents to verify software and mathematically demonstrate that it works as intended. The multi-agent AI framework has been used to prove key security properties of libsignal, the Signal protocol's reference implementation, at the machine-code level. "AlphaProof Code consists of a human-guided agent for writing Lean specifications of code, a formal semantics of AArch64 machine code, and a team of autonomous prover agents whose proofs are accepted only if Lean’s kernel checks them against the approved specification," DeepMind said. "Applied to libsignal, our agents generated about 6.5 million lines of machine-checked Lean proof code, resting on about 26,000 lines of trusted specifications and AArch64 semantics. The proofs cover Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, establishing forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy."

That's the lot for this week. Some attacks were carefully planned. Others relied on old mistakes, trusted accounts, or someone clicking the wrong thing. AI is showing up on both sides, making attacks easier to build while helping researchers find problems faster. The tools keep changing, but attackers still seem happy to use whatever works.

The good news is that some of these threats are being stopped, and defenses are slowly catching up. The bad news is that fixing a bug, removing a file, or blocking an attacker doesn't always mean the problem is gone. Sometimes the damage sticks around longer than anyone expects. Worth keeping in mind before the next batch of headlines arrives.

Standards participation: CrowdStrike leads working groups on CAEP, Shared Signals, RISC, and AuthZEN. These initiatives support interoperability and the exchange of identity risk signals across systems, helping organizations extend continuous identity security throughout their environments.

Together, these capabilities bring Continuous Identity to life, connecting visibility, risk intelligence, and real-time enforcement to help organizations stop identity-driven attacks.

CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider

CrowdStrike's approach to Continuous Identity goes beyond point-in-time authentication. By unifying identity posture management, threat detection, privileged access, and real-time enforcement on the Falcon platform, organizations can continuously assess identity risk, reduce standing privileges, and dynamically adjust or revoke access as risk changes.

CrowdStrike is redefining identity security by moving beyond traditional approaches:

Title: The XG Files: Falcon C2 Flying Under The (Browser) Radar
Context: They described it as a versatile tool for exploiting living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries (LOLBins)
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Unit 42 has identified Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē), which is a command and control (C2) framework that compromises victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites.

Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information:

Passwords

Emails

Session cookies

Communications

Falcon also served as a delivery mechanism for an implant we call Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel.

Our analysis identified the compromise of government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed in this article through the following products and services:

Advanced WildFire

Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced DNS Security

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security

Prisma Browser

Idira Endpoint Privilege Manager (EPM)

Idira Identity and Access Management (IAM)

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

Command and Control (C2), Chrome. JavaScript

Hiding in Plain Sight

Falcon C2 management panels are designed to remain semi-hidden. When accessed, the panel displays a blank page with no visible branding or login interface.

To deter casual inspection, the page disables the right-click context menu via a global contextmenu listener that calls preventDefault(). The login form also stays hidden until the F9 key is pressed three consecutive times; any other keystroke resets the counter.

Figure 1 below shows the JavaScript code for this key tracking.

Once triggered, the page displays a branded Falcon panel featuring a stylized bird logo and credential input fields. This operational security (OPSEC) mechanism ensures that it does not directly expose the login page to bots, unintended visitors and automated systems that grab webpage screenshots.

Figure 2 below shows a screenshot of the login panel.

Falcon is written in NodeJS and has two listeners. One listener is for the management panel interface on TCP port 8080 and the victim-facing listener is on TCP port 443.

On the victim-facing listener, we observed a JavaScript-based version of the classic game Tetris serving as the default page, designed to blend in further. Another instance hosted a game of Snake. Figure 3 below shows both versions.

Overlap with PeckBirdy

In January 2026, Trend Micro reported on a scripting framework dubbed PeckBirdy. They described it as a versatile tool for exploiting living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries (LOLBins).

Our comparison with PeckBirdy revealed that it shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with Falcon. Table 1 compares the URL structures of the two frameworks.

Table 1. URL structure comparison between Falcon and PeckBirdy.

Both frameworks use the same payload delivery sequence to execute HTA, HTML or JScript payloads, with the primary distinction being Falcon's inclusion of the /config/ path prefix.Both frameworks use AES for data encryption. PeckBirdy relies solely on AES with a predetermined encryption key, whereas Falcon negotiates an AES session key with the server, encrypted with RSA.Most significantly, both frameworks store their persistent session ID using the same Baidu-mimicking naming convention:

PeckBirdy writes its session ID to a browser cookie prefixed with Hm_lvt_

Falcon employs the same prefix for the same purpose, saving it as Hm_lvt_$ in the browser’s local storage and Hm_lvt__<session ID> within a browser cookie

Based on these extensive technical overlaps, we assess with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework.

The Falcon Implant

When someone visits a website affected by Falcon, the website sends a request to the Falcon C2 server. The server generates an implant uniquely obfuscated for that browser session. The implant is generated by two files: victim_common.js and victim.js.

The first file holds the configuration block described below and the second file contains common functions for communication and command execution. The two files are combined, and then passed through an obfuscation routine that XOR encodes each character in the implant with a one-byte key and converts the result into an integer.

The result is a script with a large list of integers and a small section of code to decode and execute itself. Figure 4 shows an example of the obfuscated script.

Figure 5 shows the template configuration block. The $CLIENT_IP is the victim IP address, set by the server as it generates the implant.

Victim Persistence and Tracking

The implant generates a persistent 32-character lower case alphanumeric session identifier per victim using a three-tier storage strategy designed to survive session restarts:

Browser local storage: Reading and writing a key Hm_lvt_$, likely mimicking Baidu Analytics tracking identifiers to blend with legitimate Chinese web analytics telemetry

Cookie: Setting Hm_lvt__<session ID>=1 with a path of / and an expiry date of the year 2099

Falcon extension storage cache: Checking whether a storageApi object is defined; if so, the session ID is stored there as well

The storageApi is a dictionary within the Falcon browser extension, meaning it is present only if the victim has the Falcon browser extension installed. We detail the browser extension in the Falcon Browser Extension section.

C2 Communication

The implant establishes a TLS encrypted WebSocket connection to maintain a persistent connection as long as the browser tab of the affected webpage is open. It sends a heartbeat message {"heartbeat":"1"} every minute to keep the connection alive. The implant resets the timer on every inbound message, so an actively engaged session never emits standalone heartbeats.

The code supports a fallback protocol using the Comet communication protocol. If Comet is used, payload data exchanged with the C2 server is not encrypted. The WebSocket functionality supports AES encryption in combination with the TLS transport encryption as described below.

Cryptographic Key Exchange

The implant leverages the browser's native Web Crypto API to encrypt all exchanged data using AES. If the Web Crypto API is unavailable, the implant falls back to URL-encoding and Base64. The key exchange proceeds in five steps:

Step 1: The server offers its RSA public key

Upon WebSocket connection, the server pushes a message with an action pubkey containing a 2048-bit RSA public key in PEM format, as illustrated in Figure 6.

Step 2: The client generates 256-bit AES session key material

The implant generates a 32-byte AES key and a 16-byte initialization vector (IV) using the browser's crypto.getRandomValues. If unavailable, a fallback function generates the key material from an alphanumeric string.

Step 3: The client encrypts the session key material using the server’s RSA public key

Both the AES key and IV are individually encrypted using the server's RSA public key and then Base64-encoded.

Step 4: The client sends the encrypted AES key material to the server

The client sends the encrypted key material to the server in a key_exchange message, as shown in Figure 7.

Step 5: All subsequent exchanges have their payload data encrypted with the session key material using AES-256-CBC.

Command Dispatch

Following the key exchange, the implant registers with the server by sending information about its current execution environment. Figure 8 below shows the data before encryption.

The data includes the current URL and domain of the tab within which the Falcon implant is running. The data also includes the browser's User-Agent string and client IP address (set by the backend server during implant generation).

The implant first attempts to read the remark from the browser’s local storage, specifically from the _domain_google_mark field. If unsuccessful, it then searches for the string _domain_google_mark= within the current webpage’s cookies to retrieve the remark.

If the implant uses Comet for communication, it only supports the run and nothing commands, with the latter serving no operational purpose.

The run command enables an operator to execute arbitrary JavaScript code through evaluation by calling eval. The set_remark command applies a remark (or label/comment) to the session, helping the operator organize the sessions in the management panel. It updates the remark for the fields _domain_google_mark across the browser's local storage, document cookie and Falcon extension storage.

Extension Initialization

When the extension is installed, enabled, or the browser starts, Chrome parses the extension manifest. The background service worker, background.js, runs and creates a hidden or offscreen document from the offscreen.html file.

The offscreen.html file loads offscreen.js (hereafter referred to as offscreen) and creates an iframe to load sandbox.html (which loads sandbox.js, hereafter referred to as sandbox) in parallel.

This structure is common for Chrome extensions that need offscreen documents. The sandbox acts as a code execution environment, allowing eval execution.

Offscreen starts by creating a MessageChannel message bus for communication

between extension components. It delays execution for 2 seconds to allow the message bus to be established before sending a request to the C2 server to download the Falcon implant. The code is passed to the sandbox through the message bus as shown in Figure 12.

The code is executed by appending a script tag to the sandbox.html document body. The implant code, now running inside the sandbox, establishes a WebSocket connection to the C2 server.

In parallel with the background/offscreen initialization, Chrome automatically injects content-script.js (hereafter referred to as content script) into every page visited by the victim due to its manifest definition in content_scripts.

The twitter-dm.js script is injected only if a victim visits twitter[.]com or x[.]com as defined in the manifest. The content script runs in an isolated context and only has access to the webpage's Document Object Model (DOM), but not to its JavaScript context.

To achieve full page context access, the content script injects a script tag into the page pointing to chrome-extension://<extension ID>/analytics-core.js (hereafter called analytics core). Because the analytics core file is defined in web_accessible_resources in the manifest, it is accessible to web pages and not blocked by CORS.

At this point, the extension has:

Full access to the browser's data store (via chrome.* APIs in background.js)

Full access to the context of every webpage the victim visits (via the content script and analytics core)

Web Proxy

Falcon allows an operator to use a victim’s browser as a proxy server and to use the victim’s browser data store, including session cookies and credentials for requests. An operator creates a proxy and attaches it to the victim’s Falcon session.

The operator then configures the victim’s browser with the Falcon server address and the designated proxy port. The operator is then able to send requests to the Falcon implant within the victim’s browser, with these requests encapsulated in a JavaScript snippet. They will then be sent to the victim’s browser as illustrated below in Figure 13.

The sandbox receives and executes the JavaScript. This script calls handleProxyRequest with the request data as an argument, which subsequently sends a message on the Chrome runtime message bus as shown in Figure 14.

The background service worker picks up the messages, constructs the request and sets the fetchOptions to use the victim's credential store in the request. Figure 15 below shows this, highlighted in bold.

The response from the request is Base64-encoded and returned in JSON via the C2 WebSocket. This enables an operator to browse resources using the identity of the victim, allowing for session hijacking and access to internal network resources.

Download Intercept

The extension can intercept and replace file downloads according to operator-defined rules. The operator can define broad rules targeting a list of domain and file extensions.

Figure 16 below shows an example rule that intercepts and replaces all executable downloads from google[.]com and dl.google[.]com with an operator-controlled URL.

The background service worker installs an event listener that listens for chrome.downloads.onCreated events. When detected, the background worker sends a message to offscreen over the Chrome runtime message bus, which it relays to the sandbox.

The sandbox applies the intercept rule set to the download URL to determine whether it should modify the URL. While the background service worker has the necessary privileges to intercept and replace downloads, the extension's architectural design keeps the intercept rules and C2 command processing (which requires eval execution) within the sandbox. This design necessitates passing messages across the message buses.

If the URL matches a rule, the extension cancels the original file transfer and removes the download from the Chrome download history. The new URL consists of the target and redirect URL, where the target URL is encoded and appended to the end of the redirect URL as shown below in Figure 17.

The download retains the original filename and will appear to the victim as ChromeSetup.exe while the origins will show as evil[.]com.

This technique enables an operator to achieve code execution on the victim’s system by intercepting a legitimate download and replacing it with the operator’s payload. It does so leaving little evidence that the file originated from a malicious source. The operator can use this to deploy additional malware and gain a stronger foothold in the target network.

Network Hooking

The functionality of analytics core is to install a hook for window.fetch, XMLHttpRequest.open and XMLHttpRequest.send. This hook enables the extension to intercept requests made from the current webpage and any third-party scripts loaded on the page. The operator can also define intercept rules that can replace a URL with an operator’s own URL (e.g., to hijack software updates).

For window.fetch, the hook intercepts HTTP requests that result in an HTTP 200 response and sets the content type to application/json or contains text/. The intercepted request and response data is posted to the MessageChannel as shown below in Figure 18.

For calls to XMLHttpRequest.send, the hook checks whether the HTTP response code is between 200 and 299, and whether the content type is application/json or contains text/. The hook also checks the responseType attribute to see whether it is text or an empty string.

The intercepted request and response data is posted to the MessageChannel as shown below in Figure 19.

The posted message signals the content script to relay the message from the MessageChannel onto Chrome’s runtime message bus using chrome.runtime.sendMessage as shown below in Figure 20.

The background worker picks up the message and stores it in a cache awaiting operator instructions to upload the data to the C2 server. The cache operates in a FIFO fashion and stores a maximum of 500 requests.

Discord Messages and Friends List Exfiltration

An operator can also target Discord chat messages and friend lists. They achieve this using passive network hooking described above, as Discord uses JSON in its HTTP communication. If configured, the operator can intercept requests matching a Discord URL pattern with victim data stored in a separate table.

Zalo Chat Database Exfiltration

Zalo is a chat application similar to WhatsApp that is popular in Vietnam. Falcon supports intercepting Zalo chat message databases using passive network hooking. Targeting Zalo provides additional insights into the targeted audience of the operator.

Gmail Exfiltration

While the ability to exfiltrate Gmail data is not a core functionality of the extension, it does provide an operator with the access needed to compromise a victim’s Gmail account and download email data. An operator issues a command that uploads a JavaScript to the extension, which sends a request to Gmail using the user’s Gmail session cookie to retrieve a list of authenticated users.

An operator can then select the accounts to collect data from, to be uploaded to the C2 server. This action is facilitated by the extension.

As soon as the extension is installed, loaded or the browser starts, the clipboard hijacker is actively monitoring the victim’s clipboard events. It intercepts every cut, copy and paste event by adding document listeners as shown below in Figure 21.

By default, the hijacker runs without any rules. An operator has the option to define pattern matching rules and replacements (e.g., replacing account numbers or cryptocurrency wallet addresses).

Intercepted clipboard events are passed as messages on Chrome’s message bus. These messages are picked up by the background worker and stored in a cache similar to the intercepted HTTP requests. They then await an operator command to upload the data.

The extension comes with a separate module for scraping direct messages from the X/Twitter social media platform. The module is defined in the extension manifest under content_scripts and is injected into any webpage whose URL matches the patterns *://*.twitter.com/* or *://*.x.com/*.

Possible AI-Assisted Development

The Falcon framework shows a high level of complexity in both design and capability. However, the overall code exhibits characteristics suggesting the malware authors likely used AI to assist with design and development. This conclusion is based on the coding style, including variable naming and code comments.

There are also inconsistent design choices that make little sense to a human developer. For example, the network hook for XMLHttpRequest checks for an HTTP response code greater than or equal to 200 but less than 300, while the hook for fetch checks against response.ok. Both result in the same outcome while the first is rarely, if ever, used when the response.ok shortcut exists.

While all five campaigns leveraged Falcon as their primary C2 framework, each exhibited distinct tradecraft in implant delivery and target selection, demonstrating how the operators tailored their approach to specific environments.

The operator compromised the Middle Eastern country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs Roundcube webmail portal by inserting a script tag that loads the Falcon implant. This enabled the operator to intercept credentials and monitor user sessions.

In Southeast Asian country A, the operator used Falcon to load a custom username-harvesting module. This was followed later by a fake Adobe Flash update prompt that attempted to deliver the Antino implant to pre-selected users.

Middle Eastern Country (Roundcube Webmail)

In April 2026, we observed a Falcon implant residing on the Roundcube webmail portal of a Middle Eastern Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The actor had injected a <script> tag into the portal header as shown in Figure 23.

The resource config_r5lfmqe3 returns the obfuscated JavaScript Falcon implant. This enables the actor to intercept credentials as users sign in. We observed a total of 39 Roundcube instances being affected within the target country. We have no evidence of any instances affected outside of the target country, suggesting this was a highly targeted campaign.

Title: CERT-In’s CRAFTY FALCON Advisory: AI Is the Accelerant, Your Payment APIs Are the Target
Context: CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling...
Full Text:
CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling its victims' own payment and disbursement APIs. Organizations that fixed their systems after CERT-In's first warning in October have been hit again.

The AI label will get the headlines. The attack chain tells a plainer story. Hardcoded API tokens, staging servers that share credentials with production, IP allow-lists that trust shared third-party fetchers: none of these weaknesses is new. What the AI tooling changes is the time between an attacker finding one and cashing it out, and that time is now shorter than most remediation cycles.

What CERT-In has confirmed

The latest advisory updates the previous Oct. 9 advisory. CERT-In's finance team, CSIRT-Fin, named the actor and called the campaign active and ongoing, with victims across NBFCs, digital lenders, fintechs, payment aggregators, payment service providers and crypto exchanges.

Entities that had received the earlier restricted advisories and remediated were deliberately hit again, some after incomplete cleanup, with attacks timed for holidays and weekends.

CERT-In names four publicly available offensive AI tools: ARTEX, the PentAGI multi-agent pentest system, the Cairn attack search engine and CyberStrikeAI. It doesn't attribute the actor or say how many entities were hit. Business Standard reported that researchers link at least two of the tools to China, but where a tool was written says little about who ran it.

How CRAFTY FALCON gets from a staging server to a mule account

The advisories describe four stages:

Get in. Exposed UAT and staging servers, file-upload and deserialization flaws exploited as soon as they're public, hardcoded API tokens, forged repository commits, plaintext credentials and services without MFA.

Reach production. Credentials and network paths shared with production carry the attacker across. AWS Systems Manager and Lambda then run commands through legitimate cloud channels.

Get past the app. The attacker reverse-engineers the app, calls APIs from a modified package and routes traffic through allow-listed third-party fetcher IPs that anyone can make fetch a URL.

Test, cash out, clean up. A Rs 1 transfer confirms the route. Large transfers follow to mule accounts at several banks, including through merchant settlement APIs, and crypto platforms lose wallet keys. Logs and endpoint tools get tampered with.

Because the calls come from the victim's own allow-listed infrastructure, the October advisory says they bypass KYC, beneficiary verification, balance and per-transaction limit checks. To the payment partner, the fraud looks like normal traffic.

Also read: Addressing Deepfake Risks in BFSI: Why Early Detection Is Critical

The real story: AI took away the grace period

Is "AI-driven" doing too much work here? Partly. Hardcoded tokens, plaintext credentials and missing MFA were in the October advisory before the AI tools took center stage.

What the tooling changes is cost and tempo. CERT-In says the frameworks run full attack chains on their own, refine tailored scripts in rapid succession, adapt payloads to how the target responds and rotate infrastructure within hours. Reverse-engineering one lender's app used to be a project. Now an agent can work through a target list.

That explains the re-targeting. An agent can come back, test whether the fix was complete and try the next path on a Saturday night. Patching in the next sprint assumes an attacker who gets tired. This one doesn't.

Who's exposed

Any Indian entity that can move money through an API: lenders with disbursement APIs, aggregators with settlement APIs, fintechs holding partner-bank credentials and crypto exchanges with hot wallets. You're most exposed if an internet-facing non-production environment shares anything with production, or if your payment API trusts the client app or a source IP instead of a signed, server-validated request.

What to do this week

CERT-In lists 27 actions. Start with the six that break the money path:

Cut non-production off from production. No shared credentials, keys, databases or routes, and alert on any UAT-to-production access.

Stop trusting the client and the source IP. Validate server-side, sign requests with a nonce and timestamp, use app attestation, and swap fetcher IP allow-lists for mutual TLS or scoped keys.

Retire long-lived secrets. Scan repositories and CI/CD for secrets, move to short-lived scoped tokens and rotate build and deployment tokens now.

Hold the Rs 1 pattern. Flag micro-value transfers to new beneficiaries followed by large ones, and add cooling periods and maker-checker approval on merchant settlements.

Watch the cloud control plane. Alert in AWS CloudTrail on Systems Manager sessions and SendCommand, Lambda UpdateFunctionCode in production and new IAM users, roles or keys. Default-deny server egress.

Staff the weekend and assume persistence. Lower holiday alert thresholds and verify eradication forensically.

What we're watching

The offensive tools are compromised too, though nothing ties this to CRAFTY FALCON. Researcher Badbyte recently said that a GitHub copy of ARTEX pulled a Docker image with a hidden root shell, and 62 internet-facing consoles served it between Nov. 2 and 4. It's one more reason CERT-In wants these tools banned from corporate infrastructure.

November 2026 Attack Surface Analysis

Preview-pane-triggered exploitation remains a dominant attack surface pattern for the third consecutive month, with eight Critical RCE vulnerabilities across Microsoft Office applications including Outlook and Word. CVE-2026-110043 and CVE-2026-110068 in Outlook exemplify the risk: Merely selecting a malicious message in the Reading Pane or previewing an attachment in File Explorer triggers code execution without any click or macro prompt. This attack pattern continues to be attractive to phishing operators and initial access brokers because it converts document or message delivery into reliable code execution, bypassing the user-action barrier that many enterprises treat as a training backstop.

Identity platform components face elevated risk this month with Critical flaws in both Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) and Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS). CVE-2026-119958 enables RCE against LDAP, while CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 target AD DS with RCE and elevation-of-privilege attack paths, respectively. These protocols underpin domain authentication and authorization for every joined workstation and server; successful exploitation of either can cascade to domain-wide compromise. Similar identity fabric vulnerabilities have historically been targeted by advanced adversaries seeking persistent access to enterprise environments.

Windows Hyper-V sees an unusually high concentration of privilege escalation vulnerabilities this month, with eight CVEs spanning multiple flaw classes. CVE-2026-113753, CVE-2026-113856, and CVE-2026-113860 all enable elevation of privilege within the hypervisor boundary. Hyper-V underpins Azure compute infrastructure and endpoint features such as Windows Sandbox, Credential Guard, and other Virtualization-Based Security capabilities, so the exposure extends beyond dedicated virtualization hosts to ordinary Windows endpoints with these features enabled.

Legacy network services including Server Message Block (SMB) and Print Spooler continue to draw Critical-severity RCE findings, reinforcing the persistent risk these widely deployed components carry. The unauthenticated network-reachable RCE cluster spans 14 CVEs this month, with Windows Message Queuing (MSMQ) vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-109459 and CVE-2026-116710 representing exposure on any system with MSMQ enabled. These services listen on the network by design and often lack authentication requirements for initial protocol negotiation, making any exposed instance an immediate target for opportunistic scanning. This class of legacy network service has historically been targeted in wormable exploitation scenarios.

Exploited Zero-Day Spoofing Vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook

CVE-2026-124194 is a Moderate spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook with a CVSS score of 6.5, and Microsoft confirms it is being exploited in the wild. The flaw stems from the product UI failing to warn users of unsafe actions: A specially crafted message file can cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, disclosing the victim's NTLMv2 hash.

Outlook is the default mail client across most enterprise Windows deployments, making any flaw that bypasses user safety prompts a direct initial access vector at scale. Exploitation requires the victim to open a malicious file delivered via email or another channel. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector for this particular CVE. Once the victim opens the file, Outlook silently initiates an outbound connection, and the captured NTLMv2 hash can be relayed or cracked offline to impersonate the user against other services that accept NTLM authentication.

The Moderate severity rating reflects the user interaction requirement, but the real-world exposure is broader than the score suggests. Credential disclosure flaws that require only a file open, bypass visible warnings, and yield reusable authentication material are a well-established technique in targeted intrusion campaigns. Similar spoofing primitives in Outlook have historically drawn attention from both commodity phishing operators and advanced adversaries seeking footholds in enterprise environments.

CVE-2026-112967 and CVE-2026-116928 are Critical RCE vulnerabilities in Windows services, each carrying a CVSS score of 9.8. Both allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code over the network, though they affect distinct components with different deployment realities.

Windows Search is broadly deployed and tightly integrated with Exchange for mailbox indexing, which places this flaw on an email delivery attack surface that reaches internet-facing mail infrastructure. Critical RCE Vulnerability in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)

CVE-2026-119958 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Windows LDAP with a CVSS score of 9.8. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write that allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code by sending specially crafted LDAP calls to a listening server. LDAP is the directory access protocol that underpins Active Directory. Every domain controller exposes LDAP on TCP/389 (and TCP/636 for LDAPS) by design, and the service cannot be disabled without breaking domain operations. Member servers, workstations, and applications query LDAP continuously for authentication, group policy retrieval, and object lookups, making it one of the most heavily trafficked protocols inside any AD environment.

The scope-of-impact concern is substantial. Code execution within the LDAP service on a domain controller places the attacker inside the trust boundary that every other domain resource relies on. From that position, credential extraction, replication abuse, and lateral movement to additional DCs become straightforward follow-on actions. Because LDAP is network-reachable from any domain-joined host by default, any internal foothold that can route to a DC can attempt exploitation.

Unauthenticated RCE flaws in core AD infrastructure have historically drawn rapid attention from ransomware operators and targeted intrusion actors because they collapse the gap between initial access and domain-wide compromise.

Critical Vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)

CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 are Critical vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services that both stem from incorrect authorization flaws. The two CVEs share a flaw class but differ in outcome and attack complexity.

CVE-2026-118146 carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and enables RCE. An authenticated attacker with low-level access to an affected server can send a specially crafted request and execute code without any user interaction. The authorization flaw means the server fails to properly validate that the authenticated principal should be permitted to perform the requested operation, turning a low-privilege foothold into code execution on a domain controller.

CVE-2026-118148 has a CVSS score of 7.5 and results in elevation of privilege to SYSTEM. This vulnerability has high attack complexity because successful exploitation requires the attacker to win a race condition. An authenticated attacker who can trigger the race gains SYSTEM privileges on the domain controller.

Active Directory Domain Services provides directory and authentication services for Windows enterprise domains. Domain controllers running AD DS issue Kerberos tickets, store the directory database, and process authentication and authorization decisions for every domain-joined resource. Compromise of a domain controller typically means compromise of the entire domain, since the attacker gains access to credential material and can issue arbitrary authentication assertions.

The attack surface for both vulnerabilities is any domain controller reachable from an authenticated low-privileged foothold. In most enterprise deployments, that includes every writable DC in the forest. Incorrect authorization flaws in identity platform components have historically been attractive to targeted intrusion operators because they convert commodity initial access into domain-wide compromise without requiring credential theft or additional tooling.

Critical Elevation of Privilege Vulnerabilities in Windows Hyper-V

Microsoft addresses eight Critical elevation of privilege vulnerabilities in Windows Hyper-V this month, spanning five distinct flaw classes: use-after-free (four CVEs), heap-based buffer overflow (one CVE), TOCTOU race condition (one CVE), untrusted pointer dereference (one CVE), and use of uninitialized resource (one CVE). CVSS scores range from 6.4 to 8.2, with CVE-2026-113753 at the top of the range.

The exploitation outcomes fall into two categories. CVE-2026-113753 allows an attacker to gain Virtual Trust Level 1 (VTL1) privileges, which means escaping from the normal kernel (VTL0) into the secure kernel layer that underpins Virtualization-Based Security features such as Credential Guard. Five of the remaining seven CVEs enable guest-to-host escape: An attacker operating inside a guest virtual machine can execute code on the host in the security context of the virtual machine worker process.

Hyper-V is the hypervisor layer that runs Azure compute infrastructure and powers client-side Windows features including Windows Sandbox, Windows Subsystem for Linux 2, and Virtualization-Based Security. The exposure therefore reaches both datacenter server populations and ordinary endpoints where these features are enabled.

Most of the cluster carries a high attack complexity because exploitation requires winning a race condition, which raises the practical difficulty but does not eliminate the risk. Hypervisor escapes of this class have historically attracted attention from advanced adversaries because a successful exploit compromises the isolation boundary that separates tenants in shared infrastructure and protects credential material on endpoints.

CVE-2026-113825 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in the Windows SMB Server Network Transport Driver (srvnet.sys) with a CVSS score of 7.5. The authentication requirement limits drive-by exploitation from the internet, but any attacker who has already obtained low-privileged domain credentials, or who operates from a compromised workstation, can attempt the race. Full Text:
Frontier AI is enabling threat actors to rapidly learn an environment, identify weaknesses, and chain them into viable paths to critical systems. These capabilities allow adversaries to move faster while exploiting vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and other gaps to achieve their goals.

Traditional exposure management helps organizations identify and prioritize weaknesses largely as individual risks, and periodic red team engagements only provide deeper validation at a point in time. Neither approach alone can continuously validate defenses at the speed and scale of AI-enabled adversaries. Organizations must understand not only where they are exposed, but what adversaries could achieve and whether corrective actions can strengthen their defenses.

To fight AI-enabled adversaries with AI, CrowdStrike is introducing Agentic Adversary Emulation, a new AI-powered red teaming capability powered by CrowdStrike® SafeMind. It’s now in early access.

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines specialized AI models and offensive harnesses with real-world adversary intelligence and deep knowledge of customer environments. Operating within controlled, customer-approved boundaries in production environments, it uncovers exploitable attack paths, generates prioritized remediation recommendations and compensating controls, and validates whether corrective actions have strengthened defenses.

Attack Path Discovery to Validated Defense

Reveal Potential Attack Paths

Instead of simply identifying vulnerabilities, Agentic Adversary Emulation shows how attackers could exploit and chain weaknesses across systems and identities to compromise critical assets, and where defenses can stop them. This helps security teams understand what attackers could accomplish in their environment.

Turn Findings into Defensive Action

Agentic Adversary Emulation translates these exploitable attack paths into prioritized remediation actions and compensating controls that security teams can review and deploy through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform. These may include applying patches, changing configurations, updating security policies, and creating new detections. By connecting demonstrated attack paths to corrective actions, this helps organizations focus on the weaknesses attackers can exploit and take targeted action to disrupt their progress.

Verify that Fixes Work

After corrective actions are implemented, Agentic Adversary Emulation repeats the attack simulation to verify whether those changes successfully disrupt previously identified attack paths. This helps organizations determine whether their fixes work and whether security controls can prevent adversaries from advancing toward critical assets. By connecting attack path discovery, remediation, and validation, Agentic Adversary Emulation creates a closed loop across offense and defense: attack, defend, and validate.

The CrowdStrike Advantage in AI-Powered Red Teaming

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines three core CrowdStrike capabilities to bring real-world adversary behavior into AI-powered red team testing:

Industry-leading adversary intelligence: CrowdStrike pioneered adversary-driven threat intelligence and tracks more than 290 adversaries globally. Recognized as a Leader by both Gartner and Forrester in threat intelligence, CrowdStrike draws on frontline threat hunting, incident response, CrowdStrike Falcon® platform telemetry, and intelligence on emerging threats to bring the latest adversary tradecraft directly into red team testing.

Deep knowledge of customer environments: The Falcon platform provides rich context across assets, identities, vulnerabilities, configurations, and security controls. This enables CrowdStrike to go beyond generic attack scenarios to emulate how adversaries could exploit interconnected weaknesses in a customer's environment to gain access to critical systems.

Powered by CrowdStrike SafeMind: SafeMind provides the purpose-built AI models and offensive harnesses that drive Agentic Adversary Emulation. Combining CrowdStrike’s latest adversary intelligence with deep visibility into customer environments, these systems emulate real-world adversary behavior at machine speed, continuously exploring attack paths and adapting as new weaknesses are discovered. Operating within customer-approved boundaries, they identify exploitable weaknesses, reveal how attackers could chain them together, and demonstrate what adversaries could achieve against critical assets.

During early access, CrowdStrike will work closely with selected customers to conduct controlled red teaming within defined safeguards and customer-approved boundaries, while refining the operational guardrails for safe execution in production environments.

Bringing Threat Intelligence to Smartphones

As AI accelerates adversary operations, security teams need trusted intelligence to make faster decisions, wherever they are. CrowdStrike is bringing its industry-leading threat intelligence and agentic AI capabilities to a new mobile app for iOS and Android. Available to CrowdStrike Falcon® Adversary Intelligence Premium customers, the app extends the Falcon experience beyond the desktop, providing direct access to the latest intelligence reports and the Threat Intelligence Agent.

Through the new app, customers can:

Stay ahead of emerging threats: Access expert-validated intelligence on adversaries, including their latest activities, evolving tactics, and emerging campaigns, to understand threats as they develop.

Act faster: Ask the Threat Intelligence Agent questions in natural language to quickly understand adversaries, campaigns, vulnerabilities, and emerging threats, identify what matters most, and determine what actions to take.

Make informed decisions anywhere: Access trusted intelligence and AI-driven analysis wherever decisions need to be made, without being tied to a desktop or the Falcon console.

Advancing Adversary-Driven Security for the AI Era

With Agentic Adversary Emulation and the new threat intelligence mobile app, CrowdStrike is expanding how organizations put adversary intelligence to work, from proactively simulating attacks and strengthening defenses to making informed security decisions wherever they are. Together, these innovations help defenders stay ahead of evolving threats through faster, more proactive, intelligence-driven security.

Title: New Falcon Cloud Security Innovations Secure the Cloud AI Runs On
Context: New detections combining Cloud Indicators of Attack (IOAs) with posture insights bring exposure context directly into threat detection
Full Text:
AI is accelerating both sides of cloud security. Developers and coding agents are writing more code, pulling in more open source packages, and launching more cloud and AI workloads than security teams can review by hand. Adversaries use AI to move faster, and they are targeting everything organizations build and run, from the packages in automated pipelines, to the identities that control cloud resources, to the infrastructure powering AI applications.

Security teams must keep pace on both fronts to defend against this acceleration and secure the cloud their AI runs on. CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security is built for this. It is powered by adversary intelligence tracking 290+ adversaries, so detections and risk prioritization reflect how attackers operate in the cloud. It runs on the same CrowdStrike Falcon platform that connects endpoint and identity protection with SOC operations, extending protection from developer endpoints and software supply chains to cloud workloads. Because proactive security and real-time cloud detection and response (CDR) share one platform, the exposure and attack path context teams build before an attack becomes the context analysts use to stop one.

The latest Falcon Cloud Security innovations, all now generally available, put this advantage to work from build to runtime. They help organizations stop compromised software before production, protect AI workloads and the infrastructure supporting them, and detect cloud attacks in seconds. Proactive security informs runtime defense by giving teams the context to understand risks and when to act on them. This connected defense spans business and mission-critical environments, including some of the hardest to secure.

Reduce Risk and Stop Threats Before Production

Securing the cloud that AI runs on starts with understanding where organizations are exposed and whether software entering production can be trusted. Falcon Cloud Security connects cloud risk, application context, and adversary intelligence to help teams close exposures before software is deployed.

Stop Supply Chain Threats

AI coding agents are pulling open source packages into automated builds faster than teams can review them. Adversaries can exploit that trust by compromising otherwise legitimate software. CrowdStrike observed ALTERED SPIDER compromise more than 300 software dependencies in a single day.1 A compromised dependency does not need a CVE to be dangerous, which means vulnerability scanning alone can miss the threat.

Supply Chain Security for Cloud extends the adversary intelligence CrowdStrike uses to detect and quarantine malicious packages on endpoints into container images. Falcon Cloud Security identifies compromised npm and PyPI packages during CI/CD and registry scanning, automatically reassesses previously scanned images as new threats are confirmed, and identifies affected running containers.

At deployment, the Falcon Kubernetes Admission Controller uses image assessment policies to alert on or block compromised images before they reach production. Together, endpoint and cloud protection connect the defense from package download through deployment to help teams stop compromised software.

Expand Cloud Risk and Asset Visibility

Security teams need to understand how exposures combine into opportunities for an adversary. Cloud Risks coverage in Falcon Cloud Security now extends to Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, where it connects exposure, effective permissions, vulnerabilities, and sensitive data context to identify high-risk combinations that isolated assessments can miss.

Supporting coverage expansions help teams assess more of their environment. Agentless Vulnerability Scanning for Google Cloud adds vulnerability and malware discovery for Linux-based Google Compute Engine instances without requiring additional sensor deployment. Expanded OCI inventory brings additional infrastructure, identities, and secrets into view. Together, these updates help teams account for more cloud assets and assess workloads where they cannot install an additional sensor.

Understand Applications and What Exposes Them

Cloud risk becomes more actionable when teams can connect it to the applications their business depends on. Expanded Application Security Posture Management (ASPM) brings containerized applications into Application Explorer with workload and cloud context, allowing Cloud Risks to evaluate them alongside other resources. Teams can identify combinations such as an internet-exposed Kubernetes workload running code with a remote code execution vulnerability.

New package exports map vulnerable dependencies to their associated applications, which helps teams assess blast radius and plan remediation across the application fleet. Enhanced third-party API integration findings identify external payment-service integrations and the operations applications invoke, helping teams assess exposure when a provider is compromised and uncover unauthorized integrations. The result is a clearer picture of which applications are affected and where remediation is needed.

Stop Cloud Attacks and Protect AI Workloads at Runtime

When an adversary gains access, security teams need to recognize malicious behavior, understand what is at risk, and respond while the attack is in progress. Falcon Cloud Security connects real-time detection with workload, identity, and exposure context to help defenders interrupt attacks across cloud environments.

Connect Cloud Exposure with Real-Time Detection and Response

CrowdStrike is extending Real-Time CDR to Microsoft Azure and Kubernetes, building on existing coverage for AWS and Google Cloud. Falcon Cloud Security continuously analyzes cloud audit activity as it streams, applies adversary-informed detection logic, and surfaces high-fidelity detections in seconds. Identity, asset, workload, endpoint, and adversary context helps analysts investigate and act while the attack is still in progress. All within the Falcon console, they can deny credentials or shut down compromised instances, or automate those actions with CrowdStrike® Charlotte Agentic SOAR to contain the intrusion before it spreads.

New detections combining Cloud Indicators of Attack (IOAs) with posture insights bring exposure context directly into threat detection. Suspicious behavior is evaluated alongside conditions such as dormant identities, elevated privileges, public exposure, and sensitive data so analysts can understand its potential consequences and prioritize response. A privileged action from a long-inactive identity, for example, takes on different significance when viewed alongside the conditions that could make it dangerous.

AI-based Anomaly Detection strengthens this defense by identifying suspicious behavior that predefined rules may miss. A dedicated machine learning model learns each customer’s baseline and evaluates deviations involving identities, APIs, and resources across multiple events to help uncover threats such as account takeover and API misuse. It is now available for AWS CloudTrail.

Together, these innovations connect attack behavior with exposure to help teams identify affected identities and workloads, assess potential impact, and focus response.

Protect AI Workloads and the Cloud They Run On

Securing AI requires protection for both AI interactions and the environments supporting them. Falcon Container Sensor and Falcon Guardian support for Anthropic APIs extends runtime detection to the prompt layer for supported AI workloads to help teams identify threats in AI interactions while maintaining a unified view of their environment.

Workload protection for Google Cloud Workstations brings cloud development environments into Falcon Cloud Security visibility, detection, and response workflows. Expanded AWS Bedrock AgentCore inventory complements that protection with visibility into the managed infrastructure supporting AI applications. These capabilities address distinct needs: detecting threats in supported AI interactions, protecting development workloads, and accounting for the resources behind AI applications.

Extend Protection to Regulated and Specialized Environments

Government agencies and regulated enterprises need cloud protection that reaches the environments their missions depend on. Expanded Falcon Cloud Security capabilities in US-GOV-1 and US-GOV-2 bring cloud detections, detection-rule management, and CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM workflows to GovCloud, including Kubernetes audit-log detections across Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, and Google GKE. Amazon S3 scanning in Merlin also extends sensitive-data discovery to customers in that environment.

DaemonSet support for Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Z and IBM LinuxONE, along with DaemonSet sensor support for Ubuntu Kairos, extends workload protection to specialized infrastructure. Teams can bring more of their environment into Falcon platform protection workflows without introducing separate tools, consoles, and investigation processes for each workload type. This helps close coverage gaps while reducing operational overhead.

Cloud Defense Built Around How Attacks Unfold

Securing the cloud AI runs on means understanding the software entering a build, the identities accessing cloud services, the data applications handle, and the behavior of workloads in production. Adversaries do not separate the software supply chain from the cloud identities, workloads, and data they want to reach, and defenders cannot either.

Falcon Cloud Security is built for this reality, combining CrowdStrike’s adversary intelligence with endpoint, identity, and cloud context to unite proactive security and real-time detection and response on one platform. That connection matters at every critical decision: whether to allow software into production, which exposures to fix first, and how to contain an attack already underway. Proactive context makes every real-time detection more precise and every response faster.

Expanded protection for government clouds and specialized infrastructure brings more of that connected defense to government agencies and regulated enterprises, helping protect the environments their businesses and missions depend on.

AI will keep accelerating the cloud. Falcon Cloud Security makes sure defenders accelerate with it.

Title: CrowdStrike Brings Enterprise Browser Security to the Falcon Platform
